title: India Is Building a Trade Architecture That Bypasses the U.S. The EU Deal Could Redirect $11 Billion in Exports.
excerpt: Commerce Minister Goyal is in Brussels with India's heaviest ministerial delegation in years, pushing the India-EU FTA that could shift billions in trade from America to Europe. For Indian professionals on both continents, the ground is moving.
body:
As the India-UK free trade agreement takes effect on Tuesday — making every Indian export to Britain duty-free overnight — New Delhi is already working on something far bigger. A new industry report says India's proposed free trade agreement with the European Union could redirect between $10 billion and $11 billion worth of Indian exports from the United States to Europe, reshaping the geography of Indian commerce in ways the diaspora will feel on both sides of the Atlantic.

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal landed in Europe this week leading a high-level business delegation on a five-day, three-country tour — Spain, Belgium and Finland — that is part trade mission, part diplomatic offensive. On Monday and Tuesday, he is at the India-EU Trade and Technology Council meeting in Brussels alongside External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the heaviest ministerial lineup India has sent to a European trade forum in years.

The timing is pointed. India walked away from a quick trade deal with the United States last week, betting that Washington needs New Delhi more than the other way around. With a UK pact now live, an EU agreement expected by early 2027, and India-Canada talks on a six-month clock, India is building an alternative trade architecture that deliberately reduces its dependence on a single market.

## What the India-EU FTA Changes

The numbers tell the story. India-EU bilateral trade in goods stood at $136.54 billion in 2024-25, with Indian exports valued at $75.85 billion. Trade in services added another $83.10 billion. The proposed FTA is expected to open predictable market access for Indian firms in information technology, professional services, education, financial services and construction — sectors where the diaspora has deep roots.

The EU has historically accounted for about 16.5 percent of India's total foreign direct investment. The agreement is expected to attract higher and more diversified investments into renewable energy, manufacturing, chemicals and services, creating new opportunities in precisely the sectors where Indian professionals in Europe are concentrated.

Goyal's delegation includes companies from advanced manufacturing, clean energy, digital technologies, gems and jewellery, food processing, healthcare and design — a cross-section of the industries India believes it can scale in Europe.

## The Trade Diversification Strategy

The $10-11 billion export redirect is not accidental. It is the product of a deliberate strategy by Indian trade negotiators who have watched the U.S.-India trade relationship grow more unpredictable under the current administration.

Washington has proposed new tariffs of up to 12.5 percent on dozens of nations, including India, over allegations of failing to curb trade in goods made with forced labor. India's negotiators have responded not with concessions but with leverage — rising exports (up 15 percent year-on-year in April-June despite the Hormuz disruptions), new bilateral deals, and a strengthening economic position that Goldman Sachs recently acknowledged by raising India's 2026 growth forecast to 6.8 percent.

"Indian negotiators have gained some leverage in the talks, given its strong economy, diversification initiatives with other partners, and its strategic standing in the world," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute and a former U.S. trade official.

## The Brussels Agenda

The TTC meeting in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday is focused on operationalizing the FTA, resolving pending trade issues, and deepening technology cooperation. Goyal has described the TTC as "a supplement to the free trade agreement which we have finalized" — a mechanism to smooth implementation and accelerate the benefits.

Beyond the formal agenda, the visit includes a tour of the Port of Antwerp, Europe's leading logistics hub, and the Antwerp World Diamond Centre, which sits at the heart of the global diamond value chain that Indian firms dominate. The itinerary signals India's ambition to embed itself not just in European markets but in European supply chains.

In Spain, Goyal chaired an India-Spain Business Roundtable exploring opportunities in automotive, renewable energy, railways, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, food processing and tourism. In Finland, the focus is on clean technology and digital innovation.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.1 million Indians and people of Indian origin in the European Union, the FTA could mean expanded professional mobility, easier market access for Indian service providers, and a more welcoming business environment across the continent.

The India-UK CETA that goes live on Tuesday already includes a Double Contribution Convention exempting Indian professionals working in Britain for up to five years from contributing to the UK social security system. Under the previous arrangement, about 25 percent of their salaries went toward British social security. That money will now flow into their provident fund accounts in India, earning 8.25 percent annual interest tax-free.

If the EU agreement includes similar mobility provisions — and Indian negotiators are pushing hard for them — it would represent the most significant expansion of professional opportunities for Indian workers in Europe since the IT boom of the early 2000s.

India is also in active FTA negotiations with Canada, with Goyal saying he hopes to conclude a deal within six months. Talks with Israel continue at a slower pace due to the West Asia conflict, while the proposed agreement with Peru has stalled over market access concerns.

The message from New Delhi is consistent across all these negotiations: India is not waiting for Washington to decide its trade future. It is building one of its own.

*Sources: The Hindu Business Line, Outlook Business, Reuters, Capital Market, The Indian Eye, The Freedom Press*
